articles.title: LeBron James' Reason for Wearing No. 9 Jersey at 76ers Practice Revealed in New NBA Rumors
articles.summary: LeBron James has been wearing No. 9 on his jersey during his first week of practice with the Philadelphia 76ers, a decision that reportedly has to do with a franchise icon.
articles.body:
LeBron James has been wearing No. 9 on his jersey during his first week of practice with the Philadelphia 76ers, a decision that reportedly has to do with a franchise icon.

According to Jake Fischer of The Stein Line, James chose to wear No. 9 rather than his traditional practice number of No. 6 out of respect for Hall of Famer "Dr. J" Julius Erving, whose No. 6 is retired by the 76ers.

Playing in a game-type atmosphere with the Sixers for the first time, James turned some heads with his unexpected number choice:

James will wear No. 23 for the 76ers in actual games like he has for much of his career, and he previously wore No. 6 with the Miami Heat and Los Angeles Lakers, as well as at the Olympics.

The only other known instance of LeBron donning No. 9 came during the 2004 Summer Olympics, which was the last time the United States men's basketball team failed to win the gold medal.

After spending the past eight seasons with the Lakers, James signed with the Sixers during the offseason in an effort to chase a fifth career championship.

As a 22-time All-Star, four-time NBA MVP, four-time NBA Finals MVP and the NBA's all-time leading scorer, James is already one of the greatest players in the history of basketball.

However, if he can help bring the Sixers their first championship since 1983, it would add another rich layer to his legacy.

articles.title: Fever general manager Amber Cox calls out 'attacks' on the fan base in season-ending press conference
articles.summary: Amber Cox defended Indiana Fever fans in a season-ending press conference, revealing not one fan violated the WNBA Code of Conduct this season.
articles.body: I've said it before, and I'll say it again, I don't believe there has ever been a fanbase more vilified and slandered than Indiana Fever and Caitlin Clark fans. The fanbase has been labeled as hateful by the media, opposing players and even A'ja Wilson's mom. Some media and fans, including Aces fans I spoke with outside the arena for Game 2 of the First Round of the WNBA Playoffs between the Aces and Fever, went as far as calling Fever fans "racist." This isn't just a talking point this season, either. This has been happening since Caitlin Clark was the No. 1 overall pick three seasons ago. As many of our writers have pointed out, there is a clear disdain for the Fever fan base. Our speculation is that media, players and other fan bases cannot stomach the idea that millions of new fans don't believe and vote the way they do. All that to say, Indiana Fever General Manager and Chief Operating Officer Amber Cox, who Fever fans have been calling to take a stern stance against the unfounded claims and divisive rhetoric spewed toward the Fever faithful, addressed the "attacks on the fanbase" in her season-ending press conference on Saturday. ACES' FANS SPEW UNFOUNDED CLAIMS THAT FEVER FANS ARE 'RACIST' WHILE DEFENDING A'JA WILSON After speaking to the media for over 15 minutes about her assessment of the season, including what she believed worked well, what didn't, improvements to the roster that need to be made, Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell's historic season and everything in-between, she then read a prepared statement. "I have one more thing I wanted to address," Cox started. "I just wanted to thank our Fever fan base for all of the support they continue to give us not only at home but on the road." She then stated boldly, "We have the best fans in the league," and discussed the unique mix of diversity both in cultural and ethnic background due to fans traveling from all "all 50 states" as well as "57 countries." After pointing out that the team delivered 14 of the top 15 WNBA broadcasts this season, some of which broke viewership records, with the only broadcast not in the top 15 being the WNBA All-Star game which featured three Fever players as starters (Caitlin Clark, Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston), she lowered the boom. "The attacks on our fan base have no basis in reality, and they need to stop, especially from members of the media," Cox stated while looking toward the press room, making clear she wasn’t specifically addressing the reporters in attendance. "I'm talking about media that have never been to Gainbridge Fieldhouse," she continued. "Every organization throughout the league and every organization throughout professional sports, all the way down to youth rec leagues, have to deal with occasional bad behavior from spectators." She then provided facts that are irrefutable to the media, players and others that have mischaracterized and maliciously mislabeled the Fever fan base by stating, "We did not have one fan, pointed out by a player, who violated the WNBA Code of Conduct this season. Not one fan was removed from a game." You have to remember that A’ja Wilson wasn’t the only player who tried to have a fan unfairly ejected this season. Earlier in the year, Aces point guard Jackie Young attempted to have two white male Fever fans removed from a game at Gainbridge Fieldhouse during an early-August matchup. Just like the Fever fan whom Wilson approached and verbally berated for simply pointing at her, the two men were found by security to have broken no rules. In both cases, the Amazon Prime broadcast condemned the fans’ actions without knowing the facts. To the broadcast crews, the fans were guilty until proven innocent, helping perpetuate the unfounded label that Fever fans were hateful, unruly and even discriminatory. Before I move on to some of Cox's final comments, Fever fans were also condemned for "monkey noises" made towards Angel Reese in the 2025 season. Those accusations were proven to be false. They were egregious lies meant to characterize a fanbase as racist. Even the WNBA came out with a public statement regarding the investigation that stated "The WNBA strongly condemns racism," which I felt brought some sort of validity to the accusation, whether they meant to or not. It was unhelpful for the Fever fan base, and the league as a whole. It was a witch hunt, plain and simple. Cox continued saying, "We take this really seriously and that is backed up by our security stats and the lived experience of countless fans, who we host at every game." "Our fans love this team. They're gonna cheer, they're gonna boo, and sometimes, they might point," Cox said, poking fun at the Game 2 incident involving the fan with whom the Aces forward took issue. "Fever games have always been about inclusivity. Sports are the ultimate unifier," Cox said. DETAILS EMERGE IN INCIDENT BETWEEN ACES STAR A'JA WILSON AND FEVER FAN DURING PLAYOFF GAME After she stated that she wants "everyone to be a fan of the Fever" and wrapped up her prepared statement with a "Go Fever," she allowed one more question from the media to clarify the statements she just made. "I think there have been, obviously, during our playoff series, some narratives around our fan base that are frankly not true and I thought it was important to say that no one has ever violated that fan code of conduct." Cox's final comments included a glowing review of the fans, saying, "We have a great fan base. Night in and night out, I walked out and there's 17,000 people cheering us on and they're spending hard-earned money to come here. There are little kids — boys and girls who are being inspired by our team." Cox's final point made it clear: "To be characterized in such a broad stroke is not fair." About dang time. This fan base has become a force to be reckoned with across the league because of its sheer size and passion. It’s also the reason Fever opponents are playing in NBA arenas whenever Clark and her teammates come to town. As Cox said, these fans are dedicated and spend their hard-earned money — sometimes enormous amounts of it — to see the team. Clark has inspired fans across the country and around the globe while establishing herself as a must-watch athlete. Sophie Cunningham has become a megastar by boldly stating that men have no business competing in women’s sports — all while shooting the lights out from beyond the 3-point arc. Kelsey Mitchell had a historic season, setting a record by scoring 20 or more points in consecutive games and emerging as a bona fide MVP candidate. The Fever aren't some sideshow. They are the show. They are a driver for economic and cultural change within the WNBA. That's clear. Whoever the next commissioner is needs to crack down on the divisive rhetoric. They need to build bridges and put the hammer down on the left-wing political activism and activists, who are cancerous to the league's growth and sustainability.

articles.title: Big money, bigger disaster: Minnesota exposes Michigan as Wolverines are latest example of wasted NIL funds
articles.summary: Michigan's massive NIL investment in Bryce Underwood faces scrutiny as the Wolverines drop a second straight Big Ten game to PJ Fleck's Gophers.
articles.body: Minnesota hadn’t beaten Michigan at home since 1977, but the "little brown jug" is staying in Minneapolis for the next calendar year thanks to a monster performance from the Gophers. I don't think it's hard to imagine the feelings right now from Wolverine donors, who dumped a ton of money into this roster, led by quarterback Bryce Underwood's massive paycheck he signed before stepping foot on campus in Ann Arbor. After losing to Iowa last weekend on the final play of the game, which was karma for how the Western Michigan game ended to start the season, the Wolverines have now dropped its second straight game in the Big Ten. CLOCK CONTROVERSY ALLOWS MICHIGAN WOLVERINES TO AVOID MASSIVE UPSET AGAINST WESTERN MICHIGAN And, it's not looking as if things are going to get any better for head coach Kyle Whittingham in his first season as head coach in Ann Arbor. It's a trainwreck, and Michigan donors have to be wondering how one team could waste so much money on a roster they were planning to see fight for a conference title. "Besides my marriage and kids being born, this might be the best day of my life," Minnesota coach PJ Fleck said postgame. That's right, PJ Fleck and the Gophers added to the misery on Saturday, forcing Bryce Underwood into countless mistakes, while also making this Michigan team look like a middle of the pack Big Ten squad. That's the risk schools are taking with paying top-dollar for high school athletes Welcome to college athletics in this era. Sure, some schools have decided to find their talent out of the transfer portal, more importantly at the quarterback position. But Michigan, it decided to go all-in on a high school quarterback with plenty of potential. In the process, school donors helped secure the talented 5-star with a lucrative contract that would see Underwood be paid around $10 million for the life of his deal in Ann Arbor. BRYCE UNDERWOOD ADDRESSES KYLE WHITTINGHAM'S COMMENTS ABOUT REMAINING STARTING QB AT MICHIGAN Not even two full years later, those same donors have to be kicking themselves after taking such a gamble. It's gotten so bad at Michigan that the coaching staff has thought long and hard about benching the starting quarterback due to his lackluster performances. At some point, Kyle Whittingham will have to pull the trigger and potentially move on, no matter how much money is invested in such a prized recruit at the time. It's not as if the Michigan head coach recruited him, and I promise you Whittingham does not care about ruffling feathers within the Wolverines fan base. At some point, you have to cut your losses, and that time could be coming sooner rather than later. But, once again, this is the risk you take when paying so much money for the college athlete. The only return on investment a donor is going to get out of adding funds to the NIL pool is seeing their favorite team hoist a trophy at season's end. In this case, I can almost assure you the only trophy Michigan has a chance of raising will come from a meaningless bowl game in December or early January, probably located in Charlotte or Orlando. There is nothing being shown on the field that should give Michigan fans hope for the future. Yes, I think Kyle Whittingham was the right man for the job in Ann Arbor, but this entire athletic department is a total mess, and there isn’t enough Lysol to clean it up right now. articles.title: What is latest on Marquette's Colin Porter getting a fifth season?
articles.summary: Colin Porter didn't play in Marquette's intrasquad scrimmage because his eligibility with the NCAA remains in limbo.
articles.body:
Marquette men's basketball fans are still waiting to get their first glimpse of Colin Porter.

Who knows if the transfer guard from Liberty will ever appear in a Golden Eagles uniform after suffering a setback in his legal quest for a fifth season of eligibility.

MU coach Shaka Smart held Porter out of the team's intrasquad scrimmage on Oct. 3, a day after the Kentucky Court of Appeals dissolved a temporary injunction in a lawsuit in which Porter and former Menomonee Falls standout Seth Trimble (now at Louisville) are among the plaintiffs.

That lawsuit is still pending. Porter's name is also attached to a similar lawsuit in North Carolina. Players from the class of 2022 recruiting class are seeking fifth seasons because the NCAA has allowed that for the classes that came after 2022.

"Colin is in limbo because of this fifth-year stuff," Smart said. "I guess there's stuff coming up this week with his case.

"So we're just kind of TBD with him, just trying to support him through it. He has been great. I feel bad for him that he's in limbo with this, but he's been awesome with his approach."

This a unique situation for a college basketball coach. It is under a month until MU's first game against Mercyhurst on Nov. 2 at Fiserv Forum.

"Colin is such a great kid," Smart said. "The first thing he said to me is 'I don't want to be a distraction for the team.'

"This was something that we knew when we took him that this could be up in the air, it could be in limbo. We had conversations with people in the NCAA that in this particular case are directly fighting against the fifth-year guys getting eligibility. We decided at that point that it made sense to try to do, but we knew that it wouldn't be 100%.

"Colin knew that as well. He has been phenomenal. Couldn't have been any better in the last five weeks since he's been here. Now our job is to just support the heck out of him. Obviously plan both ways. Prepare both ways, because he's somebody that would definitely make an impact on our team if he can play.

"But if he can't play, then we certainly need to plan for that scenario. Which in all honestly, he wasn't here all summer, so that was something we planning for in the first place."

articles.title: Indiana Fever Exec Condemns ‘Attacks’ On Fans After A’ja Wilson Altercation
articles.summary: Indiana Fever general manager Amber Cox is pushing back against criticism of the team’s fanbase, calling out what she described […]
articles.body:
Indiana Fever general manager Amber Cox is pushing back against criticism of the team's fanbase, calling out what she described as "attacks" in a lengthy statement. Speaking during the Fever's exit interviews on October 3, Cox defended the team's supporters amid growing scrutiny over fan behavior. Her comments come just days after WNBA MVP A'ja Wilson had a tense exchange with a fan at Gainbridge Fieldhouse, who pointed at Wilson and allegedly stepped toward her. The incident has since fueled a broader conversation online about the Fever's fanbase, and now Cox is weighing in.

Indiana Fever General Manager Defends Her Team Against 'Attacks' Online

"The attacks on our fanbase have no basis in reality." Fever GM Amber Cox closes her end-of-season press conference with a prepared statement defending the Indiana fans after receiving a lot of scrutiny online and in the media during the postseason. @WISHNews8 | @wrtv pic.twitter.com/djhacJV2oi — Angela Moryan (@AngelaMoryanTV) October 3, 2026

"The attacks on our fanbase have no basis in reality." Fever GM Amber Cox closes her end-of-season press conference with a prepared statement defending the Indiana fans after receiving a lot of scrutiny online and in the media during the postseason. @WISHNews8 | @wrtv pic.twitter.com/djhacJV2oi

Angela Moryan (@AngelaMoryanTV) October 3, 2026

A clip of Cox speaking with the media was recently shared online and showed the WNBA executive denouncing the "attacks" against her team's supporters. "They have no basis in reality, and they need to stop," she said.

Cox said the "attacks" are coming from certain media members, and that most "have never been to a game at Gainbridge Fieldhouse." She went on to say that occasional bad behavior from fans happens in every sport, and that if they violate a policy, they should be held accountable.

"But here's the fact," she added. "We did not have one fan pointed out by a player who violated the WNBA code of conduct this season. Not one fan was removed from a game. We take this really seriously, and this is backed up by our security stats and the lived experiences of countless fans whom we host at every game."

As she finished, Cox said sports are about inclusivity, and she wants the Fever's home games to be a welcoming experience for all.

Cox Is Slammed Online As Social Media Users Respond To Her Statement

It didn't take long for netizens to weigh in on Cox's statement. On Instagram, several users slammed the WNBA executive and blasted her for failing to take accountability for prior altercations. Another user asked whether her statement on the fans' reported unruly behavior was "a joke."

The popular basketball podcast " The Mid Majors " also commented and detailed their experiences with Fever fans. "Our comment section begs to differ! A whole lot of racism, bigotry, and homophobia going on over there. The stance should've been simple… that portion of the Fever fan base does NOT represent the fan base as a whole. Denounce it and call it for what it is. But I guess you can't do too much of that when you gotta keep that money rolling in."

Cox's Comments Come After A'ja Wilson Had An Intense Moment With An Indiana Fever Fan

Cox's comments come days after Las Vegas Aces star A'ja Wilson had an intense interaction with a Fever fan during Game 2 of the WNBA Playoffs.

According to The Blast , a Fever fan was seen pointing at Wilson after a physical play with Sophie Cunningham early in the fourth quarter.

Wilson addressed the moment following the game and described it as "[expletive]." She continued, "I try to play my game, keep it pushing. But if I'm just walking, cause I just got the foul, I'm chilling, and if I see a man come at me, taking steps towards me and pointing at me, I don't give a d-mn what you said. I don't give a d-mn how you said it, the tone. That is unacceptable."

The WNBA Investigated The Fever In 2025 After Reports Of Racism Directed Toward Another Player

It's not the first time the Fever's fanbase has made headlines.

A previous report from The Blast reveals that the WNBA opened an investigation after a Fever-Chicago Sky game in 2025 following reports of alleged racism directed toward Angel Reese.

"The WNBA strongly condemns racism, hate, and discrimination in all forms," the league shared in a statement. "They have no place in our league or in society."

Following a two-week investigation , the WNBA said that while it could not substantiate the claims of racism, it is committed to making the league a safe enviornment for everyone involved.

An Aces Player Received A Horrifying Message Following An Indiana Fever Game

And if that wasn't enough, the following year, Aces player Chelsea Gray opened up about a racist message she received from a fan following an Aces-Fever contest.

"People act like we just make this s— up," Gray captioned the post on her social media. "And the audacity to tell us as athletes to 'shut up and dribble.'"

Weeks later, his employer, Hilton Grand Vacations, fired the man who sent the message. "His behavior was in violation of multiple company policies and does not reflect our company's values in any," the company said in a statement, per The Blast .
